lesson.title: The Limit: What a Function Does Near a Point, Not At It
lesson.summary: A limit describes the value a function's outputs approach as the input closes in on a target number, a distinction between approaching and arriving that lets calculus make sense of functions even where direct substitution fails.
lesson.body:
A limit describes what value a function's outputs approach as its input gets closer and closer to some target number, regardless of what the function is doing exactly at that target, or even whether it is defined there at all. This distinction, approaching versus arriving, is one of the most important ideas in calculus, because it lets you make precise statements about functions at points where direct substitution fails.

Formally, we write lim(x to a) f(x) = L to mean: as x takes on real-number values closer and closer to a (from either side, but never equal to a), the outputs f(x) get closer and closer to the single number L. Because this statement is about x moving through nearby real numbers, it depends on the real number line actually being densely filled in, with no gaps, so that x can approach a through an unbroken continuum of values rather than jumping over it.

In practice, evaluating a limit usually starts the same way: try plugging a directly into f(x). If that produces a single well-defined real number, as it does for most polynomials and many other everyday functions, that number is the limit, full stop, and no further work is needed. Trouble only starts when direct substitution produces something undefined, most commonly the indeterminate form 0/0. An indeterminate form is not itself an answer; it is a signal that the expression needs to be rewritten into an equivalent form before substitution will actually work.

Consider f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1). Plugging in x = 1 directly gives 0/0, which is undefined, so f is not even defined at x = 1. But the limit only asks what happens near x = 1, not at it. For any x not equal to 1, you can factor the numerator: x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1), so f(x) = (x - 1)(x + 1)/(x - 1) = x + 1, valid for every x not equal to 1, since the (x - 1) factors cancel legally there. As x gets closer to 1, x + 1 gets closer to 2. So lim(x to 1) f(x) = 2, even though f(1) itself does not exist.

You can confirm this numerically. At x = 0.9, f(0.9) = (0.81 - 1)/(0.9 - 1) = (-0.19)/(-0.1) = 1.9. At x = 1.1, f(1.1) = (1.21 - 1)/(1.1 - 1) = 0.21/0.1 = 2.1. At x = 0.99, f(0.99) = 1.99, and at x = 1.01, f(1.01) = 2.01. The outputs are clearly closing in on 2 from both sides as x closes in on 1, matching the algebraic answer exactly.

This is the pattern behind nearly every limit computation: you cannot always just substitute, but you can often rewrite the function into an equivalent form, by factoring, simplifying, or other algebra, that agrees with the original everywhere except possibly at the troublesome point, and that new form you can substitute into directly. The limit only cares about the neighborhood of a, never the single isolated point a itself, which is exactly why a single hole in a graph never stops a limit from existing there.
